title: One Nation super plan risks $190bn bill
full_text:
One Nation’s proposal to allow workers to withdraw part of their superannuation contributions for three years could leave taxpayers facing a long-term bill of $190 billion in today’s dollars, according to new modelling from the Super Members Council (SMC).
The research follows plans announced last month that would allow workers to withdraw part of their super contributions for three years, a plan which the SMC has said will increase a reliance on the Aged Pension.
The SMC previously warned that its modelling has estimated a median full-time worker who withdrew a quarter of their super contributions for three years would retire with $25,000 less in today’s dollars, equivalent to $110,000 in future dollars.
Now, in addition, the council has estimated today’s 20-year-olds would each pay an additional $3,700 in income tax over their lifetime if the policy became law, primarily to cover higher Age Pension costs for people who withdrew their retirement savings.
Higher pension spending and lower superannuation tax receipts would together have a budget impact peaking at almost $4.5 billion a year over the long term, the modelling found.
The latest projections follow earlier council modelling examining how withdrawals could affect individual workers’ eventual reliance on the Age Pension.
A couple would be around $50,000 worse off in today’s dollars, or $220,000 in nominal future dollars.
The council said making the policy permanent would effectively wind back the super guarantee to its 2013 level of 9 per cent, reducing an average worker’s superannuation by up to $132,000 by retirement.
It also warned that accommodating withdrawals would require more superannuation assets to be held in short-term liquid investments generating lower returns, further weakening retirement savings.
That modelling estimated a median full-time worker aged 25 who withdrew 3 per cent of their contributions for three years would receive $6,923 after contributions tax, while generating an additional $14,000 in lifetime Age Pension costs.
This amounted to $2.02 in additional pension spending for every dollar withdrawn by the modelled worker, rather than an estimate of the policy’s overall cost.
SMC chief executive Misha Schubert warned early withdrawals would compound the financial pressures facing Australians while reducing their retirement savings.
“Australians are facing real cost of living and housing pressures but damaging everyone’s retirement savings and driving up inflation further through early super withdrawals would just make those pressures worse.”
“Your super is not designed to be an ATM or to solve politicians’ policy problems. A policy like that won’t just make you much poorer in retirement – it will also hand you, your kids, and your grandkids a bigger tax bill to pay more in pensions if other people take their super out early,” Schubert said.
“That higher bill to taxpayers will also make it harder to fund the essential services that battling Australians rely on – hospitals, medicines, schools, roads, and emergency drought and flood relief.”
The council said Australia was on track to have the lowest pension spending in the OECD, with Age Pension expenditure projected to decline from 2.3 per cent of GDP today to 1.8 per cent by 2066.
It warned the proposal could reverse that trajectory by increasing reliance on the pension as retirement savings were depleted.
According to the council, the projected taxpayer cost would be more than double that of the COVID-era Early Release of Super scheme, under which almost $38 billion was withdrawn.
The SMC cited research presented at an RBA workshop which found those withdrawals triggered a sharp spending response, including on gambling, alcohol and tobacco, furniture and food delivery.
author: Adrian Suljanovic
heading: Superannuation and Investments
